summary.text: A 37-year-old woman was diagnosed with melanoma in the lymph node region after excision of a massive congenital nevus on the left upper arm. Left axillary lymphadenopathy was removed, with melanoma in 49/52 lymph nodes. Adjuvant vemurafenib ran from 2011 to 2014, a left mastectomy was done for locoregional recurrence, and discontinuation was agreed given her wish for fertility preservation.

A 2015 PET scan detected pleural recurrence at the costovertebral region, and removal of chest wall nodules was required. First-line nivolumab was started and 55 cycles were completed by 2018. A 2017 CT showed lesion reduction, but progression to left retroperitoneal and supraclavicular lymph nodes was evidenced by July 2018 on CT and CT-PET.

Ten days into second-line dabrafenib with trametinib she was urgently admitted with hyperthermia and abdominal pain, and treatment was temporarily discontinued. On resumption one month later a diffuse nonpruritic maculopapular rash and fever resolved with oral steroid and antihistamine. CT in November 2018 showed complete response. In January 2019 arthralgias, cramps and fever required further discontinuation and improved with prednisone 25 mg; G2 leuko-neutropenia was observed.

Targeted therapy was restarted in May 2019, followed by stable CT findings. Three months later a leg rash and fever prompted discontinuation and steroid with good response; despite dose reduction, recurrent fever and further complications led to a decision to switch to encorafenib and binimetinib. Left eye discomfort and reduced visual acuity prompted an ophthalmologic consultation that found cystoid macular edema; about three months later posterior uveitis was treated with Ozurdex.

Given negative findings for recurrence and worsening uveitis, the team decided to proceed with left-eye treatment while continuing rigorous oncologic follow-up. A November 2020 CT showed no signs of secondary lesions, the macular edema was completely reabsorbed, and fluoroangiography showed stable foci with vasculitis and hyperfluorescence regression. She is currently disease-free, with a complete response lasting over 5 years.
